clinicalPearls: A bilateral granulomatous panuveitis accompanied by neurological, auditory, and integumentary features, reflecting an autoimmune attack on melanocyte-containing tissues
More common in pigmented populations, particularly those of Asian, Hispanic, Middle Eastern, and Native American descent
A prodromal phase with headache, meningism, tinnitus, and dysacusis often precedes the ocular disease
The acute uveitic phase causes bilateral serous (exudative) retinal detachments, disc oedema, and choroidal thickening
Later convalescent features include a 'sunset glow fundus' from choroidal depigmentation, poliosis, vitiligo, and alopecia
Cerebrospinal fluid pleocytosis in the acute phase supports the diagnosis when the picture is incomplete
Prompt and prolonged systemic corticosteroids, often with steroid-sparing immunosuppression, help prevent chronic recurrent disease and preserve vision
reference.pathophysiology: Vogt-Koyanagi-Harada disease is a T-cell-mediated autoimmune disorder directed against antigens associated with melanocytes, affecting melanocyte-rich tissues including the uvea, meninges, inner ear, and skin. A genetic predisposition linked to certain HLA types, possibly triggered by a viral or other environmental insult, leads to autoreactive T lymphocytes targeting melanocytic proteins. Granulomatous inflammation of the choroid produces exudative retinal detachments and, in the chronic phase, depigmentation of the choroid and skin, giving rise to the characteristic sunset glow fundus, poliosis, and vitiligo.
additionalDifferentials: Acute posterior multifocal placoid pigment epitheliopathy
Infective causes such as syphilis and tuberculosis
additionalInvestigations: Dilated fundus examination and slit-lamp assessment for panuveitis and exudative retinal detachment
Fluorescein angiography showing multiple pinpoint leaks and pooling of dye in subretinal fluid
Optical coherence tomography demonstrating serous retinal detachment and choroidal thickening
Indocyanine green angiography to assess choroidal inflammation
Lumbar puncture showing cerebrospinal fluid lymphocytic pleocytosis in the acute phase
Serology to exclude syphilis, tuberculosis, and sarcoidosis
redFlags: Bilateral rapid visual loss from exudative retinal detachment
Meningism and neurological signs in the prodromal phase
Recurrent or chronic anterior uveitis indicating inadequately treated disease
Development of complications such as glaucoma, cataract, or choroidal neovascularisation
reference.prognosis: With early, aggressive, and sustained immunosuppression many patients retain good vision, but delayed or insufficient treatment leads to chronic recurrent granulomatous uveitis with cataract, glaucoma, subretinal fibrosis, and permanent visual impairment.
pitfalls: Tapering corticosteroids too quickly and precipitating chronic recurrent disease
Confusing exudative retinal detachment with central serous chorioretinopathy and treating inappropriately
Failing to exclude sympathetic ophthalmia in a patient with prior ocular trauma or surgery
Not recognising the prodromal meningeal or auditory symptoms as part of the syndrome
Overlooking infective mimics such as syphilis before starting immunosuppression
management: Early high-dose systemic corticosteroids, often intravenous pulses followed by a slow oral taper, as the mainstay of acute treatment
Early introduction of steroid-sparing immunomodulators such as mycophenolate, azathioprine, methotrexate or ciclosporin to prevent chronic recurrent disease
Biologic therapy with anti-TNF agents such as adalimumab or infliximab for refractory or recurrent disease
Monitor for and manage ocular complications including cataract, glaucoma and choroidal neovascularisation
Audiological and neurological assessment for auditory and meningeal features in the acute phase
Prolonged, sustained treatment with long-term ophthalmology follow-up to avoid relapse
Uveitis specialist and rheumatology multidisciplinary care
